record.paper_title: On some open problems of number theory
record.original_question: When positive perfect powers are arranged in increasing order, must the difference between consecutive terms tend to infinity?

artifact.self_contained_problem: A positive integer n ≥ 2 is called a perfect power if there exist integers a ≥ 1 and k ≥ 2 such that n = a^k. Let 1 < p_1 < p_2 < p_3 < ... be the sequence of all positive perfect powers (with 1 sometimes adjoined) listed in strictly increasing order. Prove or disprove: the consecutive gaps p_{n+1} - p_n tend to infinity as n → ∞. Equivalently, show that for every positive integer N there are only finitely many pairs of perfect powers whose difference equals N.
artifact.status_search_result: Pillai's conjecture (1936/1945), which is equivalent to the statement that gaps between consecutive perfect powers tend to infinity, remains an open problem. Only the special case k = 1 (Catalan's conjecture) has been settled by Mihăilescu (2002). The general statement would follow from the abc conjecture but is not proved.

status_evidence.title: Pillai's Conjecture -- Wolfram MathWorld
status_evidence.snippet: A general difference of perfect powers ... is an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Perfect Powers: Pillai's works and their developments (Waldschmidt)
status_evidence.snippet: Pillai conjectured that the distance between two consecutive elements in the sequence of perfect powers tends to infinity; this remains open and follows from abc.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is equivalent to gaps tending to infinity and is open.

status_evidence.title: Catalan's conjecture - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Mihăilescu proved Catalan's conjecture (the case difference = 1) in 2002; Pillai's more general conjecture remains unsolved.
status_evidence.claim: Only the difference-1 case is resolved.
